sentences.text: Zhenyuanlong suni was a mid-sized dromaeosaurid covered in feathers over its entire body, including large wings and long tail feathers. It possessed a furry coat of simple filaments on most of its body, while the wings and tail featured more complex structures.
The preserved skeleton measures 122.6 cm in length because the rear half of the tail is missing. Including the long tail feathers, the animal may have reached a total length of 2 meters in life.
Despite having small arms, Zhenyuanlong had the shortest arm-to-leg length ratio of all known dromaeosaurids, except for the basal Mahakala and the giant unenlagiine Austroraptor.
Body feathers were preserved only as small impressions on the front and back of the neck, yet the wing feathers were very long, measuring more than twice the length of the upper arm bone.
Zhenyuanlong was roughly the size of a condor but weighed twice as much, at approximately 20 kilograms.
Zhenyuanlong is the largest known non-avian dinosaur with complex feathers and the first short-legged dromaeosaurid with a feathered morphology.

Zhenyuanlong is known from only one fossil specimen of the species Zhenyuanlong suni. The single known specimen preserves a nearly complete skeleton with skull and jaws, long tail feathers, and large wings. The holotype specimen JPM-0008 was found in the Yixian Formation in Liaoning Province, China.
The fossil was discovered by a local farmer near Sihedang in Jianchang, Liaoning Province.
Zhenyuanlong suni was named and described in 2015 by Lü Junchang and Stephen Brusatte.

Despite having modern-looking wings, Zhenyuanlong was likely too large and heavy to fly or glide. Authors suggest Zhenyuanlong was likely too large to fly, emphasizing the need for biomechanical modeling to determine the function of its wings.
The presence of large wings on a non-flying dromaeosaur raises questions about their function.
The genus Zhenyuanlong and the species Z. suni were both named by Lü and Brusatte in 2015.

Zhenyuanlong is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae. Cladistic analysis places Zhenyuanlong in the same evolutionary position as other Liaoning dromaeosaurids like Changyuraptor, Graciliraptor, Microraptor, Sinornithosaurus, and Tianyuraptor.

Zhenyuanlong lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Asia. Zhenyuanlong lived during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 113 million years ago. The genus Zhenyuanlong existed from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
It is impossible to determine if Zhenyuanlong's body feathers were simple filaments or complex structures with a central vane.
Due to preservation issues, the symmetry of the tail feathers cannot be fully assessed, though they resemble those of other bird-like dinosaurs.
Because the tail tip is missing, it cannot be ruled out that Zhenyuanlong had a fan-like structure at the end of its tail.

It is debated whether Zhenyuanlong retained flight capabilities through inertia or unknown adaptive reasons despite its size. Researchers suggest the most viable hypothesis is that Zhenyuanlong used its wings for sexual display, such as threatening rivals or courting mates.

Researchers suggest that the most viable function for Zhenyuanlong's wings was sexual display, such as threatening rivals or courting mates, similar to how a peacock uses its tail. Alternative hypotheses for Zhenyuanlong's wings include protecting eggs in the nest or some form of arboreal gliding.
